anatomy.lede: Under the leaves is a seahorse-like fish: an armoured body of bony plates, a tube for a mouth, and fins so small and clear that it seems to drift rather than swim.

hotspots.label: Snout
hotspots.text: The long, thin, pipe-like snout has no teeth. It sucks in tiny prey whole, working much like a pipette.

hotspots.label: Face
hotspots.text: Markings on the face differ between individuals. Divers have used photographs of them to recognise the same seadragon for at least 11 months.

hotspots.label: Leafy appendages
hotspots.text: The leafy appendages are bony and stand away from the body, so scientists have been able to attach tracking tags to them without harming the fish.

hotspots.label: Spines
hotspots.text: Each bony plate of the body carries a long, sharp spine that may help defend the seadragon.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: A small, transparent dorsal fin on the back ripples to push the fish along. Seadragons have lost the tail fin and the pelvic fins.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail makes up about half the total length. In males, eggs are carried attached to its underside.

body.lede: Seadragons feed, defend themselves and breed in ways shared only with their seahorse and pipefish relatives.

systems.title: No teeth, no stomach
systems.text: Leafy seadragons have neither teeth nor a stomach, so they feed almost constantly on mysid shrimps, other small crustaceans and larval fish.

systems.title: A suit of bony plates
systems.text: The body is covered in bony plates, each bearing a long, sharp spine, giving this fragile-looking fish a suit of armour.

systems.title: Male pregnancy
systems.text: It is the male who carries the eggs, attached to a brood area on the underside of his tail, for the six to eight weeks until they hatch.

genome.lede: In 2022 researchers published chromosome-scale genomes of a male leafy seadragon and a female weedy seadragon, the first major genetic resources for these fish.

findings.title: Missing growth-factor genes
findings.text: Seadragons, seahorses and pipefishes have lost the genes fgf3 and fgf4, which other vertebrates use in forming teeth, limbs and skin outgrowths. This may be linked to their toothless jaws and unusual bony armour.

findings.title: A genome full of repeats
findings.text: Seadragon genomes are unusually dense in repetitive DNA, with recent bursts of 'jumping genes' (transposable elements). They also have divergent non-coding DNA near a developmental gene involved in skin outgrowths.

findings.title: Two separate populations
findings.text: DNA from 71 wild seadragons shows two main groups, one in Western Australia and one in South Australia. Genetic diversity is moderate to low, and especially low in the west.

mind.lede: Tracking and photo-identification show the leafy seadragon is a homebody, spending most of its time standing still in a small patch of reef and seagrass.

studies.title: Tracked by sound
studies.text: Nine adults fitted with ultrasonic tags mostly stayed within home ranges of up to 5 ha. Short bursts of movement were separated by long still spells, by day or by night.

studies.title: Known by their faces
studies.text: Over 14 months, divers identified nine individuals from their facial markings and resighted them months apart in the same area, about 57 seadragons per hectare.

studies.title: Seasonal gatherings
studies.text: Seadragons are usually solitary and move into deeper water in winter. In late winter they gather in shallow bays to pair and mate.

survival.lede: A slow, fragile fish with few defences, the leafy seadragon survives by not being noticed.

tactics.title: Hiding as seaweed
tactics.text: Leafy appendages, the ability to change colour and a gentle swaying motion make it look like drifting weed.

tactics.title: Spines
tactics.text: Sharp spines on the bony plates may deter a predator that sees through the disguise.

threats.title: Losing kelp and seagrass
threats.text: The kelp and seagrass habitats seadragons need have been retreating throughout their range.

threats.title: Pollution and fishing
threats.text: Coastal development, pollution and fertiliser runoff damage their habitat, and some are taken as bycatch or by poachers.

threats.title: Warming seas
threats.text: Rising water temperatures from climate change may also affect them.

life.lede: Seadragon life begins on the father's tail, and the young emerge looking nothing like their leafy parents.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays 250–300 eggs, each about 4 mm across, onto the underside of the male's tail.

stages.name: Brooding
stages.text: The male carries the eggs, each held in its own small cup in his skin, until they are ready to hatch.

stages.name: Hatching
stages.text: He releases only a few young at a time, so a whole brood can take hours or days to hatch.

stages.name: Fry
stages.text: Newborn fry have very short snouts and no leafy appendages, and stay close to the bottom for about two days.
